title: Watch Norway’s Lice-Zapping Robots Protect Salmon Farms - Nautilus
gist: Salmon lice are a costly, legally mandated problem for Norwegian salmon farms, having grown resistant to drugs while traditional delousing harms fish and cleaner wrasses are hard to keep alive — the setup for robotic lice-zapping solutions (not detailed in excerpt).

insights.claim: Salmon lice are the scourge of Norwegian salmon farmers who raise fish in Atlantic net pens, and removing the parasites is required by law.
insights.so_what: Lice control is a structural cost and mortality driver for Norwegian salmon producers.
insights.quote: Removing them is required by law, but it’s a real pain.
insights.locator: These parasites are also the scourge
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: Salmon lice have become resistant to pharmaceutical deterrents, and traditional delousing via hot water baths, scrubbing and rough handling can damage or kill the fish.
insights.so_what: Drug resistance and treatment mortality create demand for non-chemical tech like robotic lasers — a niche aquaculture-tech opportunity.
insights.quote: They’ve become resistant to pharmaceutical deterrents
insights.locator: Removing them is required by law
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: Some Norwegian farms use cleaner wrasses to eat the lice, but the fish have proved difficult to keep alive.
insights.so_what: Biological controls are unreliable, reinforcing the case for automated alternatives.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
